course_description:
This course will provide students with the skills and knowledge necessary to research and develop fiction across a range of genres. The emphasis is on understanding creative practice, thoughtful gathering of source material, synthesising ideas, and writing and editing a substantial piece of fiction.

Purpose of the Course

This course will provide students with the skills and knowledge necessary to research and develop ideas for fiction (usually a short story), and understand creativity and its contexts.

Course Goals

On completion of the course, students will be familiar with a wide range of approaches suitable for creative writing projects, and will be able to use research to produce a finished piece of fiction.

Teaching and Learning Modes

WRIT7050 is taught as a weekly 2.5 hour seminar featuring researching and writing strategies, group activities and discussions, individual creative exercises, and student presentations.

Expectations and Obligations

You will need to have reliable access to e-mail, and will need to check for messages regularly.ﾠPlease note that, if you send an e-mail from a hotmail or similar account, the university's anti-spam firewall may intercept your e-mail, and your tutor may not receive it.ﾠYou are expected to check the course's Blackboard site regularly, and contribute to discussion groups where necessary.

learning_outcomes.description: Plan and conduct research to inform the drafting, revision, and editing of creative writing or related projects, demonstrating ability to apply craft techniques and integrate developed ideas.
Analyse and evaluate practice and theory underpinning contemporary creative writing or related projects, including stylistic, structural and rhetorical strategies employed their production.

Investigate the ethical, creative, and professional challenges in the development and delivery of a new creative writing or related-project, demonstrating awareness of diverse perspectives, integrity, and social responsibility.
Assess significance of trends, debates and industry contexts that shape creative practice across a range of written forms.
Collaborate effectively in workshop settings through provision of constructive, discipline-specific feedback that demonstrates critical thinking and sensitivity to working with others.

assessment_details.task_description: Through completion of a series of in-class tasks and activities, this assessment will enhance your understanding of the practice, processes and challenges of initiating, researching and developing new creative works. Activities to be completed – outlined on LearnUQ – range from writing exercises, workshopping, and group discussion, which includes sharing exercises, works-in progress, and insights on craft, process and artefact development and submission. These activities will facilitate understanding and consideration of form, storytelling, elements of narrative, and broader issues and concerns including cultural difference, intersectionality and intercultural, ethical and relational communication. Completion of in-class tasks and activities (between Weeks 4 to 12) will be awarded up to 8 points per class. Your best marks from five weekly tutorials will be added together to give you a final mark out of 30. Your mark should reflect a ‘meaningful contribution’, where it aids your own and the work of your peers, and or adds to, augments, the co-creation of knowledge and understanding. While your best five tutorials will make up your final mark, we encourage you to participate in as many tutorials as you are able. There are 8 opportunities across the semester, each worth 8%. Only your best 5 results count toward your mark (/40%) for the assessment. While there is flexibility to miss up to 3 sessions — for illness or any other reason — with no penalty and no documentation required, we would encourage you to attend as many seminars as possible. There are no opportunities to re-take an individual exercise, and no alternative assessment is available except in the specific circumstances set out below. As this is an internal course, you must make yourself available to complete each exercise at the scheduled date, time and venue. The writing activities are handwritten, closed-book tasks: no written material, electronic material or electronic devices may be used. All such items must remain in your bag or under your desk, and all electronic devices must be switched off or in airplane mode. If a device emits any noise, you may be subject to an allegation of misconduct and the item may be confiscated for the duration of the exercise. You may bring suitable writing implements (in a clear container), water in a clear bottle with the label removed, and disposable earplugs. The discussion activities will be delivered during seminar and are also closed-book tasks: no written material, electronic material or electronic devices may be used. All such items must remain in your bag or under your desk, and all electronic devices must be switched off or in airplane mode. If a device emits any noise, you may be subject to an allegation of misconduct and the item may be confiscated for the duration of the exercise. You will share 'workings' and reflections in class as you undertake written activities. Your mark will reflect a ‘meaningful contribution’ to class discussion. Your contribution is 'meaningful' where it adds to, augments, the co-creation of knowledge and understanding. This may include (but is not limited to): asking thoughtful and relevant questions; sharing appropriate and relevant responses or commentary; engaging in peer feedback; or assisting peers in their completion of assigned activities. While your best five tutorials will make up your final mark, we encourage you to participate in as many tutorials as you are able. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Essay
assessment_details.task_description: Write a short essay that critically assesses the form you intend to employ in the production of the creative work submitted for your final assessment. For example, if you intend to submit a folio of 'flash' fiction, you might consider the work of Lydia Davis and examine the impacts the form has on word choice and storytelling; if you intend to submit a new short story, you might consider essays by Poe, Carver or Moore; if you intend to submit a short comic or sequential art, you might consider drawing on the work of Scott McLoud; or if you intend to submit an excerpt from a longer piece of literary journalism, you might consider Tom Wolfe's influential discussion on the form, or examine its use in writing about climate crises or sport? You must consult with your tutor on the topic of your essay. Use citations with MLA style, include a reference list with at least 6 items. To be submitted: Essay (1000 words (excluding refs) ) Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Stories Overview of the course and ideas, or at least some discussion where stories come from. Learning outcomes: L03, L05
Week 2: Form The relationship between Form and Content and the shapes and sizes our stories might assume. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L05

Week 3: Elements of Narrative A blast through the building blocks of storytelling and the ways they operate: the tour will take in character and setting, order and purpose, voice and dialogue. Learning outcomes: L02, L04, L05

Week 4: Short Fiction If it's fiction and it's shorter than a novel, it's likely regarded as short form, then we must distinguish the novella from the short story from even shorter, flashier kinds of fiction. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04, L05
Week 5: Creative Non-Fiction 'True stories, well told', apparently, but what does that mean? And, what do they look like? Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04, L05
Week 6: Words and Pictures Whether you know them as graphic novels or sequential art, comics are often regarded as the perfect blend of image and text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05
Week 7: Genre – Realism Following a brief introduction to genre – we'll look at one of the most common, realism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05
Week 8: Historical Incursions Integrating story research. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Week 9: Story Problems Narrative problems and approaches to resolving them. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L05
Week 10: Feedback – Give and Take Developing and delivering productive feedback and how best to take it on board. Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 11: Workshopping Stories I Small group workshopping and feedback. Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 12: Workshopping Stories II Small group workshopping and feedback. Learning outcomes: L01, L04, L05
Week 13: Prepping for Submission Focus on writing, editing, polishing and prepping final assessment for submission. Learning outcomes: L01

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
